opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's one of the trickiest parts of this whole thing. If you look at polling, the public cares about a lot of different things at once: job loss, deepfakes, kids and chatbots, copyright, privacy, energy use, and somewhere in there the "will this thing get out of control" question. These concerns don't always point in the same direction, and they have very different constituencies behind them.

So my expectation is that regulation will be messy and patchwork, at least for a while. You'll get a lot of narrow, issue-specific rules, like deepfake laws, child safety rules, disclosure requirements, and some sector-specific things in healthcare or finance. Those respond to concrete harms people can already see, which is what politics is good at reacting to.

What I worry about is that the risks I spend most of my time on, models that are deceptive or pursue goals we didn't intend and are increasingly capable of acting autonomously, aren't very salient to most people yet. They're hard to explain, and there usually isn't a visible victim until something has already gone wrong. So there's a real chance that regulatory attention gets used up on the visible issues while the frontier-risk questions get comparatively little.

That said, I don't think it has to be either/or. A lot of the infrastructure you'd want for the catastrophic risks also helps with the everyday concerns: transparency about what developers are testing for, third-party evaluations and auditing, incident reporting, and some way for the government to actually understand what's happening inside frontier labs. Those are fairly "boring" governance mechanisms, and they're relatively defensible across the political spectrum, because they're about knowing what's going on rather than banning things.

My best guess is that the realistic path looks like this: a baseline of transparency and evaluation requirements for the most capable models, building up state capacity to understand the technology, and then a lot of reactive regulation after incidents. The honest version is that much meaningful policy will probably come in response to some event that makes the risks concrete. So part of what we in the evals and safety community should be doing is having good, well-tested proposals ready, so that when the window opens, the response is sensible and not just panicked.

r001.rationale: The candidate predicts messy, issue-specific regulation driven by competing public concerns, with visible issues taking attention away from less salient frontier risks.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that I don't expect regulation to be a clean reflection of what the public wants, because the public doesn't want one thing. If you look at polling, people simultaneously want AI to cure diseases and make their jobs easier, and they're also worried about job loss, about misinformation, about losing control. Those preferences pull in different directions, and the political process doesn't resolve that into some coherent philosophy. It resolves it into whatever is salient at the moment.

So my model is that regulation will be mostly reactive. Something goes visibly wrong, there's a wave of public attention, and lawmakers respond to that specific thing. We saw a version of this with deepfakes, where nothing much happened for years, and then once there were high-profile cases involving real people, suddenly there was a lot of legislative activity. I'd expect the same pattern for things like AI-enabled fraud, or if there's a serious cyber incident where an AI system is clearly implicated.

The thing I worry about is that the risks I care most about, like loss of control or models that are strategically deceiving their developers, don't produce the kind of incident that makes people react in time. By the time you have a dramatic, legible event, you might already be past the point where regulation helps much. So you end up with a mismatch: the regulation follows the visible harms, and the harms that matter most might not be the visible ones.

What I think is more realistic, and what I'd push for, is regulation that doesn't try to settle the big value questions at all. Instead it focuses on things most people can agree on regardless of what they want from AI: transparency about what frontier labs are doing, requirements to publish safety frameworks and actually follow them, third-party access for evaluations, incident reporting. Those are fairly boring, procedural things, but they're compatible with a lot of different public preferences. Someone who's excited about AI and someone who's scared of it can both agree that the companies building it should be honest about what their systems can do and what safeguards exist.

And then the hope is that this kind of infrastructure means that when the public mood does shift, or when there is an incident, policymakers have real information to act on, rather than scrambling with no visibility into what's actually going on inside these labs. I think the realistic goal isn't to get the public to converge on a single view of AI. It's to make sure that whatever they end up wanting, the system is in a position to actually respond to it.

r001.rationale: The response says public preferences pull in different directions and predicts regulation will react to salient visible harms, leaving less visible serious risks insufficiently addressed.

astra-6.text:
I expect it to be quite messy. People want very different things from AI, and sometimes the same person wants things that are in tension: they want access to very capable systems, but they also want guarantees that those systems won’t cause harm. So I don’t think there’s going to be one regulatory approach that everyone is happy with.

But you don’t need agreement on everything to make progress. You can disagree about what AI should ultimately be used for and still agree that companies should test their systems before deploying them, or that there should be accountability when something goes wrong. I’d expect a lot of the useful regulation to be around those more concrete questions.

The harder part is that both the technology and public opinion can change much faster than regulation. A particularly beneficial application could make people much more enthusiastic; a serious incident could push them in the opposite direction. So I’d want a framework that can adapt as we learn more, with enough technical expertise inside government to distinguish meaningful safeguards from requirements that just sound reassuring.

r001.rationale: The candidate predicts regulation will be messy and that no single approach will satisfy everyone, but does not say divergent preferences will make regulation poorly targeted.

sol-6.1.text:
I expect it to be quite messy. People want very different things from AI: some want the benefits as quickly as possible, others are worried about their jobs, and others care about privacy or catastrophic risks. And those preferences don’t necessarily translate into a coherent regulatory agenda.

But you don’t need everyone to agree on the whole picture to get useful regulation. Someone who is excited about AI and someone who is very worried about it might both want companies to test their systems properly and report serious incidents. So I’d expect a lot of regulation to emerge around specific problems where there’s enough agreement to act.

The harder question is what happens when safety measures impose real costs or slow deployment. That’s where the disagreements become much more consequential. My guess is that we’ll get an uneven process: some sensible rules, some rules that miss the point, and a lot of revision as people see what these systems can actually do.

r001.rationale: The response says differing preferences may prevent a coherent regulatory agenda and predicts an uneven process with some rules that miss the point, communicating that divergent preferences will produce poorly targeted regulation.
